notes: **Days and months take a small letter.** *lundi*, *mars*, *décembre* — unlike English. Capitals only at the start of a sentence.

**Le lundi means "every Monday".** Without the article, *lundi* means "this Monday" or "last Monday", depending on the sentence. *Je travaille le lundi* = I work on Mondays; *je travaille lundi* = I'm working on Monday. One tiny word that changes your whole schedule.
**Dates use le + an ordinary number.** *Le quinze mars* ("the fifteen March"), not *le quinzième mars* — unlike English "the fifteenth". The one exception is the 1st: *le premier mars*.

**Years are read as one whole number.** 2005 = *deux mille cinq*, 1998 = *mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-dix-huit*. French doesn't split them into two numbers the way English does ("nineteen ninety-eight").

**Soixante-douze = 72**, literally "sixty-twelve". French runs out of number names at 69 and starts adding. This is the part of French foreigners laugh at most — and Belgians and the Swiss do use the saner *septante* and *nonante*. But in France, the counting system rules.
**Du mardi au samedi** = from Tuesday to Saturday. Notice the merging: *de + le = du*, *à + le = au*. The same merging you used in Unit 8.
**Bonne journée** is said when parting in the morning or afternoon: "have a nice day". Its relatives: *bonne soirée* (evening), *bon week-end*, *bonne semaine*, *bonnes vacances*.

grammars.title: Numbers above 60 — a system that counts
body: Up to 69, everything makes sense. From 70 up, French stops naming and starts adding.
after: ⚠️ *Quatre-vingts* takes an s only when it stands alone at the end. As soon as another number follows, the s disappears: *quatre-vingt-un*, *quatre-vingt-cinq*.
*Et* appears only in 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and **71**. Not in 81 and 91: *quatre-vingt-un*, not *quatre-vingt-et-un*.
Hundreds: *cent, deux cents, trois cents*. The s disappears here too when another number follows: *deux cent cinquante*. *Mille* never takes an s: *deux mille*, *dix mille*.

grammars.title: Saying the date
body: One pattern for everything: le + number + month + year. Note that French writes the day before the month.
after: Asking the date: *Quelle est la date aujourd'hui ?* or *On est le combien ?* The answer is *on est le quinze* or *nous sommes le quinze*.
Months take **en** or **au mois de**: *en mars*, *au mois de mars*. Years take **en**: *en 2026*. Seasons take *en* except spring: *en été, en automne, en hiver*, but *au printemps*.

blocks.text: The French week starts on **lundi** (Monday), not Sunday. Calendars, timetables and planners all put Monday in the first column.

blocks.title: Seasons and holidays
items: *au printemps*, but *en été*, *en automne*, *en hiver*. Only spring takes *au*.
*Bonnes vacances !* — have a good vacation. *Bonne année !* — happy New Year.

exercises.prompt: Write the numbers out in words.
Write out the full date in words (day/month).
Fill in le, or write « rien » (nothing) if no article is used.
items: Je travaille ____ lundi, tous les lundis.
____ mardi prochain, je vais à Paris.
____ samedi, je suis allé au cinéma.
Je fais du sport ____ mercredi, chaque semaine.
My date of birth is March fifteenth.
The library is open Tuesday to Saturday.

answers: soixante-douze — quatre-vingts — quatre-vingt-onze — soixante-huit — quatre-vingt-dix-neuf — deux cent cinquante
le premier janvier — le quatorze juillet — le vingt et un août — le trente et un décembre — le quinze mars deux mille vingt-six
